name: Toyota Avalon
engine: 3.5L naturally-aspirated V6 (2GR-FKS), 301 hp — 2.5L hybrid, 215 hp combined — (2021+ added a 2.5L I4 with AWD, 205 hp)
drivetrain: FWD (V6 and hybrid) · available AWD on the 2.5L I4 (2021+)
reliability: 9/10 — the fifth-gen Avalon is essentially a longer, plusher Camry, and it inherits the same excellent dependability. The 301 hp 2GR V6 is one of Toyota's most proven engines, the 8-speed automatic is well-sorted, and the hybrid system is long-lived and returns an easy 40+ mpg. The main documented item is the 2020 Denso low-pressure fuel-pump recall shared across many brands. It is a quiet, comfortable, quick full-size sedan that will run for a very long time.
cost_to_own: Insurance: Average · Maintenance ~$450/yr · The V6 asks for a bit more fuel, while the hybrid is genuinely frugal for a big sedan · Resale is good, though full-size sedans depreciate more than Toyota's SUVs
popular_mods: Quality all-season or winter tires — the biggest comfort and safety upgrade on a big FWD sedan
All-weather floor liners and tasteful wheels
Sound-deadening and OEM-plus dampers on higher-mileage cars for an even quieter ride
The factory TRD trim shows how far owners take the sportier look
Honest take: the Avalon is about quiet comfort and a strong V6 — money is best spent on tires and upkeep, not power
oil_type: 0W-20 full synthetic (0W-16 on the hybrid four — check the cap)

generations.4th Gen XX40 (2013–2018 US): The comfortable, understated Avalon — 3.5L V6 with a 6-speed automatic, plus a 2.5L four-cylinder hybrid. Roomy and durable, if anonymous.
generations.5th Gen XX50 (2019–2022 US): A bolder, sportier-looking redesign on the TNGA-K platform — 301 hp V6, an efficient hybrid, available AWD (2021+ four-cylinder), and a genuinely plush, quiet cabin. The first Avalon with a TRD trim.
generations.Discontinued after 2022: Toyota retired the Avalon in the US after 2022; the rear-drive-based Crown effectively replaced it at the top of the sedan range.

common_issues: 2020 Denso low-pressure fuel-pump recall — industry-wide; confirm it is closed by VIN
Big-sedan depreciation — full-size sedans lose value faster than Toyota's SUVs, which is actually good news for used buyers
More road noise on the sportier Touring/TRD trims with larger wheels
Infotainment on early XX50 cars felt dated; later years improved it
The V6 is thirstier than the four-cylinder rivals — the hybrid is the frugal choice
maintenance_tips: Keep up with the specified synthetic oil on the Maintenance Minder
Service the 8-speed automatic fluid on schedule despite 'lifetime' claims
Confirm the fuel-pump recall and any open recalls by VIN
On the hybrid, keep the traction-battery cooling intake clear and the 12V battery healthy
Budget for tires and brakes; otherwise this is low-maintenance Toyota V6 motoring

engine.detail: A 301 hp 3.5L V6, a 2.5L hybrid, or (2021+) a 2.5L four with AWD - the 2GR V6 is one of Toyota's most proven engines.
engine.watch: Very reliable; routine synthetic oil is about all it asks. The V6 is thirstier, so the hybrid is the frugal pick.

drivetrain.detail: FWD (V6/hybrid) or AWD (2021+ four), with an 8-speed automatic on gas cars or an e-CVT on the hybrid.
drivetrain.watch: A few early-2019 V6 cars show mild low-speed hesitation/shift feel - never enough for a recall; service the fluid on schedule.

fuel.detail: Regular unleaded with port/direct injection and an in-tank electric fuel pump.
fuel.watch: Confirm the 2020 Denso low-pressure fuel-pump recall is closed by VIN - industry-wide; a failing pump can stall the engine.

electrical.detail: 12V battery, touchscreen infotainment, and Toyota Safety Sense driver aids.
electrical.watch: Some owners report a weak 12V battery or corroded terminals, and early XX50 infotainment felt dated - keep the battery healthy.

body.detail: Plush, quiet full-size cabin, often with a power rear-window sunshade on upper trims.
body.watch: The powered rear sunshade can grind or fail - a common owner complaint, but it's a cosmetic annoyance, not a reliability worry.
